rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all eight peaks while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The retention window and critical-pair resolutions will guide adjustments to gradient slope, solvent range, and temperature.
Change temperature alone to test selectivity in the central cluster and the nearly coeluting final pair. The short initial elution window leaves room to slow the gradient later if needed.

Halve the gradient slope at the better-performing temperature to test whether the three unresolved pairs separate as their elution compositions shift. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes.

A slightly shallower gradient should improve the remaining critical pair while preserving the resolved central cluster. Extrapolating from the previous runs places the last peak just below 10 minutes, making this a promising route to CRF 1.0.

The shallower gradient drove the critical pair toward coelution, so return to the best gradient and adjust temperature instead. A 5 °C decrease tests whether selectivity can resolve that pair without losing separation in the central cluster.

At 60 °C, a slightly steeper gradient should separate the pair that converged when tG increased to 24 minutes. This tests whether that improvement outweighs the expected small loss of resolution in the central cluster, while keeping elution comfortably below 10 minutes.

The best run is only slightly short of full resolution. Raising the starting organic fraction while keeping tG fixed tests a modest slope and selectivity adjustment that may lift the central pair above 1.5 without merging the later critical pair.

This gives a slightly shallower slope than injection 7, targeting the two marginal central pairs while retaining separation in the later pair. The final organic fraction remains above the observed elution window, so all eight compounds should elute well before 10 minutes.

Reduce the slope slightly from 0.04583 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute to lift the marginal central pairs above 1.5 while preserving the later pair’s small resolution margin. All peaks should elute during the gradient and remain comfortably below 10 minutes.

Injection 9 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark and test a shorter elution window. Raising the starting organic fraction also makes the gradient shallower, which may preserve the central separations while bringing the last peak forward.

Retain injection 9 as the maximum-score method; raising phi0 sacrificed a central separation. Test the low-temperature selectivity regime to look for an alternative route to full resolution with a shorter elution window.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope at 25 °C to test whether both unresolved pairs improve. This low-temperature branch could provide full resolution with a last peak near seven minutes, while injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

The slower gradient worsened the central critical pair at 25 °C, so test a steeper gradient to reverse that trend and shorten elution. This will also establish whether the late pair remains the main obstacle on this faster branch; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Test a modest temperature increase on the faster low-temperature branch to measure whether its two critical pairs gain selectivity. Injection 9 already achieves the maximum CRF and remains the fallback if this shorter method cannot reach full resolution.
Shift the starting composition to test selectivity in the single unresolved central pair at 30 °C while shortening the elution window. Injection 9 remains the fully resolved, maximum-CRF benchmark.

Test a substantially shallower gradient to see whether the central pair separates again after an elution-order crossing. The higher starting organic fraction should offset some of the added retention; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Further reduce the slope to test whether the central pair gains resolution beyond its apparent crossing, while the other pairs have substantial resolution margins. The elevated starting composition should keep the last peak below 10 minutes; injection 9 remains the maximum-CRF benchmark.

Lower temperature by one step to move the final pair away from its apparent convergence on this shallow-gradient branch. This tests whether the central separations survive while the late pair improves; injection 9 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten the newly fully resolved low-temperature method. The accompanying shallower slope may preserve its critical central separation while bringing the last peak closer to the faster injection 9 benchmark.

Test one further increase in starting organic fraction to see whether the central pair separates on the other side of its near-coelution at phi0 0.30. This could produce a shorter fully resolved method; injection 9 remains the established maximum-score choice.
Injection 20 is now the fastest fully resolved method, with a minimum resolution of 1.75. Shorten its gradient to test whether that margin permits faster elution while retaining the maximum CRF.

The shorter gradient preserved full resolution and improved the minimum resolution, so test a further reduction to 10 minutes. This should shorten the elution window while checking whether the central and late pairs retain R ≥ 1.5.

Shorten the fastest fully resolved method by one grid step to seek earlier elution. The late pair’s R of 1.85 provides some margin, while the central pair will also be monitored as the gradient steepens.

Test one more gradient-duration step to establish the speed limit for full resolution on this branch. Injection 23 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method if either marginal pair drops below 1.5.

Preserve injection 23’s fully resolving slope of 0.05 organic fraction per minute while shortening the programmed gradient by lowering its endpoint. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, retaining CRF 1.000 and the approximately 4.14-minute last-peak time.
